props.title: Stolen Kisses
props.initialSlug: Young soldier pursues love and odd jobs in Paris

sections.content: Stolen Kisses (1968) marks the third installment in François Truffaut's Antoine Doinel series, following The 400 Blows (1959) and the short film Antoine and Colette (1962). Jean-Pierre Léaud returns as the now 20-something Antoine, bringing his signature blend of awkward charm and restless energy to a character navigating early adulthood. The film perfectly captures the French New Wave's ability to mix comedy with profound observations about youth and romance, while maintaining a lighter touch than its predecessors.

sections.content: What sets Stolen Kisses apart is its playful approach to the coming-of-age narrative. Unlike the heavy drama of The 400 Blows (1959), this film embraces life's absurdities as Antoine stumbles through various jobs - from hotel clerk to private detective - while pursuing Christine Darbon. The film's structure mirrors Antoine's meandering journey, with Truffaut employing his characteristic mix of documentary-style realism and whimsical storytelling devices that influenced later works like The Graduate (1967) and Harold and Maude (1971).

The film's influence extends beyond the French New Wave, establishing a template for depicting young adult uncertainty that echoes through contemporary cinema. You can trace its DNA in works like Frances Ha (2012) and The Worst Person in the World (2021), where characters similarly navigate the messy space between adolescence and adulthood. Truffaut's genius lies in making Antoine's confusion feel both specifically French and universally relatable. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Coming-of-Age Cinema

sections.content: Stolen Kisses represents a crucial bridge between the raw angst of early New Wave cinema and the more nuanced character studies that would follow. Its influence can be seen in films like My Night at Maud's (1969) and Claire's Knee (1970), where Eric Rohmer adopted a similar approach to examining young love and moral choices. The film's impact on modern independent cinema is equally significant, with directors like Noah Baumbach and Greta Gerwig often citing Truffaut's influence on their own explorations of young adulthood.
